content: 1. Simplify the description of a product or condense it into a few words. 2. Organize data into tables, such as usage rates or volumes. 3. Reduce the spacing between paragraphs, but maintain spacing between lines. 4. Use abbreviations only when they are universally understood. 5. Relocate information to less crowded areas of the label. 6. Adjust column widths so that paragraphs align closer to the column edges. 7. Increase the number of columns where necessary, such as in safety text. 8. Use a separate or integrated leaflet for additional information. 9. When translating text into another language, account for variations in space requirements between languages. 10. Avoid using overstickers to amend label information unless absolutely necessary and approved by regulatory authorities. 11. Ensure stickers do not obscure other valid label information. Use of Color 12. Red is a universally recognized warning color and should only be used for hazard symbols, hazard color bands, or safety advice headings, in accordance with the Globally Harmonized System (GHS). 13. The label’s color scheme should ensure that hazard symbols are clearly visible. 14. For optimal contrast and readability, use black text on a plain white background. 15. On leaflets and brochures, color can enhance visual appeal and understanding. 16. Important parts of drawings can be emphasized with contrasting colors, but excessive or overly intense colors should be avoided as they may distract from the intended message. 17. Red should always be placed on a white background and never on other colors like yellow. 18. Recommended color combinations include: black on white, black on yellow, red on white, green on white, and white on blue. 19. Color bands on labels can indicate the acute toxicity of a product and must stand out clearly from the rest of the label. Signal Words and Hazard Statements 20. All labels must include appropriate signal words and hazard statements based on the product’s hazard classification. 21. The GHS recommends using harmonized signal words such as DANGER for severe hazards and WARNING for less severe hazards. 22. WHO classifications use signal words like VERY TOXIC, TOXIC, HARMFUL, and CAUTION, which differ from GHS terminology. 23. If WHO classification is used, its signal words should be applied instead of GHS terms. 24. Hazard statements describe the nature and degree of the product’s hazards and should be included on the label. 25. Signal words and hazard statements should be placed close to hazard symbols to enhance understanding. Precautionary Statements and Warnings 26. Precautionary statements describe measures to minimize or prevent adverse effects from exposure, improper handling, application, or storage of the product. 27. These statements should accompany hazard communication elements like symbols, signal words, and hazard statements. 28. Precautionary statements are not internationally harmonized and may vary by country. National legal requirements should always be followed. 29. In the absence of national requirements, the GHS provides suggested precautionary statements for prevention, response, storage, and disposal. 30. Precautionary statements should address identified hazards and risks and be placed near related hazard statements on the label. 31. General precautionary statements, such as KEEP LOCKED AWAY AND OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN, WASH AFTER USE, and DO NOT eat, drink, or smoke when using this product, should always appear on pesticide labels. 32. If personal protective equipment (PPE) is required, explicit instructions like WEAR GLOVES WITH EVERY USE should be included. Use of Symbols, Pictograms, and Illustrations 33. Hazard symbol pictograms must be used to visually represent the product’s hazards, as defined by the GHS. 34. These symbols should be black on a white background with a red frame and must be at least 10x10 mm in size. 35. Precautionary pictograms should visually convey key safety measures for handling, applying, or storing the product. 36. Pictograms should always complement text and never contradict or obscure it. 37. Only use recommended pictograms unless locally developed ones are proven effective. 38. Essential precautionary pictograms include those for washing after use and keeping the product locked away from children. Tactile Warnings 39. Pesticides supplied to the general public should include tactile warnings for the visually impaired. 40. The word PESTICIDE should be printed in Braille on labels for public-use products. 41. A tactile warning of danger is required for products classified as dangerous by national authorities, especially those in WHO hazard classes 1a and 1b or GHS acute toxicity categories 1 and 2. First Aid and Medical Advice 42. Labels must provide first aid instructions for various routes of accidental exposure. 43. Include the statement: If medical advice is needed, have product container or label at hand. 44. Provide information on antidotes and where to obtain further treatment advice. Accidental Spills Advice 45. Labels should include instructions for cleaning up accidental spills, tailored to the product’s active ingredients and formulation. 46. Recommendations may include keeping people away from the spill area, using PPE, avoiding environmental contamination, and absorbing liquid spills with materials like sawdust or clay. 47. Spilled substances should be swept into containers, and leaking containers should be emptied into appropriate replacements.
